title: From Holberg’s Time (Holberg Suite)
hook: A Norwegian Romantic dresses up in a periwig: five old-style dances for strings, written for the 200th birthday of Bergen’s most famous writer.

painting.title: Scene from Ludvig Holberg’s The Lying-in Room
painting.pairingNote: A crowded scene from one of Holberg’s comedies, in the silks and lace caps of his century; like Grieg, the Danish painter looked back from the 1800s to Holberg’s time and brought it to life.

facts: Ludvig Holberg (1684–1754), born in Bergen, became the great playwright of Denmark–Norway, sometimes called the Molière of the North. Grieg was also from Bergen, and in 1884 the town celebrated Holberg’s 200th birthday.

For the festivities Grieg wrote a cantata for male voices and this suite for piano, which he played himself in December 1884. He then arranged it for string orchestra, and in that form it was first heard in Bergen in March 1885. The string version is the one everyone knows.

The subtitle is “Suite in the olden style”. Grieg borrowed the dances of Holberg’s day, the early eighteenth century, and said he had modelled the piece on the French keyboard composers of that time. He joked that it was a “periwig piece”. It is an early example of [[neoclassicism|neoclassicism]]: old forms, filled with Grieg’s own Romantic harmony and Norwegian warmth.

A Baroque [[suite|suite]] usually opens with a prelude and continues with dances. Grieg keeps that plan, and he lets the string orchestra divide into many parts and solos, so the sound is much richer than any Baroque band.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a galloping prelude (I), a stately sarabande (II), a gavotte with a bagpipe musette (III), a sorrowful air (IV), a sparkling rigaudon (V).

movements.heading: Praeludium
movements.title: Praeludium
movements.summary: The best-known movement: a bright, energetic prelude driven by a galloping rhythm of repeated chords from start to finish. In the piano original this was a stream of broken chords; for strings Grieg turned it into this pulsing pattern, with a broad, bold tune singing out beneath it.

mainIdeas.name: The gallop
mainIdeas.description: repeated chords in a long-short-short rhythm, passed through the upper strings.

mainIdeas.name: The tune
mainIdeas.description: a broad, rising melody in the lower strings, under the gallop.

stops.hear: A galloping rhythm of repeated chords, with a broad tune rising beneath
The music softens and moves into new keys
Shimmering chords in the divided violins while the violas pluck rapid scales
stops.happening: One of Grieg’s new string colours, a [[pizzicato|pizzicato]] line under held chords

stops.hear: The opening gallop and tune return

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: A bright, emphatic close

notice: Follow the galloping rhythm. It almost never stops, yet the music never sounds mechanical, because the harmonies keep changing under it.

movements.heading: Sarabande
movements.title: Sarabande
movements.summary: A slow, dignified [[sarabande|sarabande]], the old Spanish-French dance in three beats. Grieg divides the strings into many parts, so the chords sound thick and glowing. In the middle a solo cello comes forward, warm and singing.

mainIdeas.name: The dance
mainIdeas.description: a noble melody in slow triple time, with the weight often on the second beat.

mainIdeas.name: The cello’s song
mainIdeas.description: a solo cello leads in the middle section, richer and darker.

stops.hear: A slow, stately melody over full, glowing chords
A solo cello sings, warm and deep
The opening melody returns, fuller

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: The music quietens and settles on a soft chord

notice: Count the beats: one, two, three. Listen for how the second beat often feels heavier than the first, the old sarabande step.

movements.heading: Gavotte – Musette
movements.title: Gavotte – Musette
movements.summary: Two French dances in one. A graceful [[gavotte|gavotte]] frames a [[musette|musette]], a country dance named after a small French bagpipe: under its tune the low strings hold a long, buzzing note, as a bagpipe’s drone would.

mainIdeas.name: The gavotte
mainIdeas.description: a poised, courtly tune in G major.

mainIdeas.name: The musette
mainIdeas.description: a quicker, rustic tune in C major over a [[drone|drone]].

stops.hear: A poised, elegant dance tune
A bit quicker and rustic; under the tune a low note keeps sounding, like a bagpipe
The elegant gavotte returns

stops.label: Last 10 seconds
stops.hear: A neat, light ending

notice: In the musette, listen to the bass. It hardly moves, just as a bagpipe’s drone cannot.

movements.heading: Air
movements.title: Air
movements.summary: The emotional heart of the suite: a slow, grave song in G minor, marked “Andante religioso”. The form is Baroque, but the dark, sometimes feverish harmony and the long, sighing lines are Grieg’s own.

mainIdeas.name: The air
mainIdeas.description: a long, sorrowful melody in the violins over a gently pulsing accompaniment.

mainIdeas.name: The climax
mainIdeas.description: the melody climbs and the harmony grows more intense, almost passionate.

stops.hear: A slow, sighing melody in the violins over soft, pulsing chords
The melody is heard again, fuller
The line rises; the harmonies grow richer and more intense
stops.happening: The middle, building to a climax

stops.hear: The opening melody returns

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The music grows quieter and ends softly

notice: Listen for the moments where the harmony suddenly darkens or brightens. That is where the nineteenth century shows through the eighteenth-century costume.

movements.heading: Rigaudon
movements.title: Rigaudon
movements.summary: A quick, cheerful [[rigaudon|rigaudon]], an old French dance in two. A solo violin and a solo viola race along together while the rest of the strings accompany them with plucked chords. A slower, more wistful middle section in G minor gives contrast before the dance returns.

mainIdeas.name: The rigaudon
mainIdeas.description: a bright, leaping tune in duet for solo violin and solo viola.

mainIdeas.name: The middle section
mainIdeas.description: a calmer, singing tune in G minor for the full strings.

stops.hear: Two solo instruments, a violin and a viola, dash through a bright tune over plucked chords
All the strings join in, louder
Slower and more wistful: a singing tune in G minor
The quick duet returns

stops.label: Last 10 seconds
stops.hear: A quick, bright ending

notice: In the rigaudon, try to pick out the two solo players from the plucked accompaniment, like two dancers in front of a crowd.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Marriner and the Academy recorded the suite in May 1970 in London’s Kingsway Hall, and the first LP paired it with Dvořák’s Serenade for Strings.

threads.title: Old forms, new feelings
threads.body: Each movement borrows an eighteenth-century dance, but the harmony, especially in the Air, belongs to Grieg’s own time.

threads.title: Bergen’s two sons
threads.body: Grieg wrote it to honour a writer from his own city, a century and a half older.

threads.title: A string orchestra of many voices
threads.body: Grieg divides the sections, gives solos to single players and mixes bowed and plucked sounds, so a small band sounds like a full orchestra.
